details:
Project Details — ARES
ARES (Autonomous Reconnaissance & Exploration System) is a mobile-first Mars exploration and EVA planning prototype focused on investigating boxwork formations in lower Mount Sharp, Gale Crater.
ARES brings several parts of a planetary exploration workflow into one connected workspace. Users can explore a Martian map, examine scientific images and geological information through the Science Intelligence & Image Laboratory, define exploration objectives, and organize proposed EVA routes and field observations. Its purpose is to help users move from studying a location to preparing a more informed exploration plan.
One of ARES's key benefits is that it makes scientific information easier to access and understand. It distinguishes between REAL DATA, CALCULATION, and SIMULATION, helping users recognize the difference between published scientific evidence, derived information, and hypothetical scenarios. This encourages transparency and helps prevent simulated information from being mistaken for actual measurements.
The intended impact is to demonstrate how planetary maps, scientific imagery, and mission-planning concepts can work together to support future human exploration of Mars. ARES is designed as a decision-support prototype, not an autonomous navigation or safety system.
The project was developed using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, with Leaflet for interactive mapping and Three.js explored for 3D terrain development. GitHub was used for code management and website hosting through GitHub Pages. Development also involved AI-assisted brainstorming, coding support, and debugging using ChatGPT and Claude. The interface was designed with mobile accessibility in mind.
ARES is creative because it connects planetary science with practical astronaut field-planning in a single student-built system. Rather than presenting a Martian map alone, it considers how explorers might use scientific evidence to decide what to investigate and how to organize an EVA.
Our team considered scientific reliability, the clarity of information, mobile usability, exploration objectives, terrain-related challenges, limited mission resources, and the importance of clearly communicating the project's current capabilities and limitations. We aim to keep ARES accessible while maintaining a strong connection to real planetary science.
